lead: Every levelling method repeats one step: from a set-up, the backsight on a known point and the foresight on a new point give the new point's RL. The methods differ in how the steps are strung together and what the run is for. Differential levelling carries a height to a distant point through change points. Fly levelling is a quick run of backsights and foresights to bring a height to the work, and check levelling closes the run back on a known benchmark to measure the error. Profile levelling takes many intermediate sights along and across a line, so that a road, canal or pipeline can be drawn as a section and its cutting and filling worked out.
prereq: You need: HI = RL + BS and RL = HI − reading from Levelling terms, and an adjusted level from Levels and their adjustments.

sections.h3: Simple, differential, fly and check levelling

blocks.text: Simple levelling uses one set-up: the difference of level between two points both visible from one station is BS − FS. When the points are far apart, the ground is too steep for the 4 m staff, or obstacles block the view, the run is split by change points. This is differential levelling (compound levelling): each change point is read as a foresight, the level moves on, and the same point is read as a backsight.
ΣBS − ΣFS = RL(last point) − RL(first point)
blocks.where: ΣBS is the sum of all backsights and ΣFS the sum of all foresights in the run, in metres. This checks the arithmetic of the run; it cannot detect a misread staff.

blocks.text: Fly levelling is a quick differential run with long, balanced sights and no intermediate sights, to bring a benchmark's height to a site. Check levelling tests earlier work: it ends back on the starting benchmark or on another benchmark of known RL. The closing error e is the observed RL of the closing benchmark minus its known RL.

The permissible closing error is written e = C√K mm, with K the run length in km and C set by the class of work (a few mm for precise levelling, more for ordinary work). An acceptable e is shared out: correction at a point = −e × (set-ups up to it ÷ total set-ups), or in proportion to distance. A larger e means the run is repeated.

Profile levelling (longitudinal sectioning) finds ground RLs along the centre line of a road, railway, canal or sewer, pegged every 20 m or 30 m and at changes of slope. Each set-up has a backsight, intermediate sights on the pegs in view, and a foresight on a change point. RL plotted against chainage, with an exaggerated vertical scale, is the longitudinal section (L-section).

Cross-sections are levelled at right angles to the centre line at each peg, at set offsets left and right. The engineer draws the formation line (the proposed finished level) on the L-section. At each peg, depth of cutting = ground RL − formation RL when positive; depth of filling = formation RL − ground RL when the ground is below formation. Formation RL at chainage x on a falling gradient of 1 in n is RL₀ − x ÷ n.

items: Instrumental: collimation error (cancelled by equal sights), a sluggish bubble, a loose tripod head, a staff of wrong length.
Natural: curvature and refraction on long sights, wind, heat shimmer, the tripod or a change point sinking.
Personal: bubble off centre while reading, parallax, a tilted staff (always reads too large), misreading the metre, booking in the wrong column.

Precautions: sights under about 100 m and balanced; check the bubble at every reading; rock the staff and take the smallest reading; change points on firm, sharp objects; book before moving and check on site.

examples.question: Profile levelling was done along the centre line of a proposed road from a BM of RL 85.250 m. The readings were: BS 1.420 on the BM; IS 1.865 at chainage 0, 2.310 at 20 m and 2.945 at 40 m; FS 3.280 at 60 m (change point); BS 0.865 at 60 m; IS 1.540 at 80 m and 2.105 at 100 m; FS 2.660 at 120 m. The formation starts at RL 84.200 m at chainage 0 and falls at 1 in 50. Find the ground RLs, the depth of cutting or filling at each peg, and where the formation meets the ground.
steps: Formation falls 1 in 50, that is 0.400 m per 20 m: 84.200, 83.800, 83.400, 83.000, 82.600, 82.200 and 81.800 m at chainages 0 to 120.

The cut changes to fill between 80 m (cut 0.115 m) and 100 m (fill 0.050 m). Assuming straight ground between pegs, the formation meets the ground at 80 + 20 × 0.115 ÷ (0.115 + 0.050) = 80 + 13.94 = 93.94 m.
examples.answer: Ground RLs from 84.805 m at chainage 0 to 81.595 m at 120 m; cutting from 0.605 m down to 0.115 m up to 80 m, filling of 0.050 m and 0.205 m at 100 m and 120 m; the cut-fill (zero) point is at chainage 93.94 m.

examples.question: Check levelling was run from BM A (RL 100.000 m) to a temporary benchmark T and back to A, with four set-ups of roughly equal length, 1.6 km in all. Set-up 1: BS 1.325 on A, FS 2.040 on CP1. Set-up 2: BS 0.985 on CP1, FS 1.760 on T. Set-up 3: BS 2.115 on T, FS 1.090 on CP2. Set-up 4: BS 1.905 on CP2, FS 1.428 on A. The specification allows 12√K mm. Find the closing error, decide whether the work is accepted, and give the corrected RL of T.
steps: Permissible error = 12√1.6 = 12 × 1.265 = 15.2 mm. Since 12 mm < 15.2 mm, the work is accepted.
Correction per set-up = −12 ÷ 4 = −3 mm. T is reached after 2 set-ups, so its correction is −6 mm: RL of T = 98.510 − 0.006 = 98.504 m.
examples.answer: Closing error +12 mm, within the permitted 15.2 mm, so the run is accepted; the corrected RL of T is 98.504 m.

traps: Ending a profile run with an intermediate sight. The last reading of every set-up, including the final one, is a foresight.
Thinking the check ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL proves the field work. It only checks the arithmetic; a misread staff still balances. Closing on a known benchmark is the field check.
Applying the whole closing error to the last point. It is shared in proportion to set-ups or distance, so T in the example gets −6 mm, not −12 mm.
Getting cut and fill the wrong way round: cut when the ground is above formation, fill when it is below.

quiz.q: What is fly levelling, and when is it used?
quiz.a: A quick differential levelling run with only backsights and foresights, used to bring a benchmark's height to a site or to get an approximate height.

quiz.q: Why is the vertical scale of a longitudinal section exaggerated?
quiz.a: Height changes along a road are small compared with its length; a vertical scale about ten times the horizontal makes rises, falls and depths of cut and fill readable.

quiz.q: A check run of 2.5 km closes with an error of −21 mm. The specification allows 12√K mm. Is it accepted?
quiz.a: Permitted = 12√2.5 = 12 × 1.581 = 19.0 mm. |e| = 21 mm > 19.0 mm, so the run is rejected and must be repeated.

quiz.q: Ground RL at chainage 140 m is 81.020 m. Using the worked example's formation (84.200 m at 0, falling 1 in 50), find the depth of cut or fill.
quiz.a: Formation = 84.200 − 140 ÷ 50 = 81.400 m. Ground is lower, so fill = 81.400 − 81.020 = 0.380 m.

quiz.q: In the worked example, the staff at chainage 60 m sank 8 mm between the foresight and the next backsight. Which RLs are wrong and by how much?
quiz.a: The backsight taken after sinking is 8 mm too large, so the second HI and every RL from it (80, 100 and 120 m) are 8 mm too high. RLs up to 60 m are correct.

beyond: Not for the exam. Road projects now take the L-section and cross-sections from a terrain model built by total station, GNSS or drone survey, and design software draws the formation, computes cut and fill and produces the mass-haul diagram. Long national levelling lines are still run with precise digital levels and invar staffs, with closing limits of a few millimetres per square root of a kilometre. Search for mass-haul diagram, precise levelling and digital terrain model.

figure.caption: The longitudinal section of the worked example. The road is in cutting where the ground line is above the formation line and in filling where it is below; the two lines cross at chainage 93.94 m.
